paragraphs: The standard complaint against biography is that it imposes a shape. A life is lived forward and blindly, one thing after another, with nobody knowing what any episode will turn out to have been the beginning of. A biography is written backward from an ending already in hand, and in the writing every early episode acquires a significance it could not have carried at the time. The childhood illness becomes the origin of the physician's later patience. The abandoned first manuscript becomes an apprenticeship rather than a failure. From this the complaint concludes that biography is a species of falsification, and that an honest form would be one that refused to make the pieces fit.

I propose to grant the premise without reservation and then watch where it leads. Suppose it is entirely true that no episode of a life carries its meaning at the moment of its occurrence, and that significance is conferred afterward, by somebody looking back with the ending in hand. The conclusion still does not follow. What follows is that retrospective conferral is not the peculiar vice of biographers but the condition of any account of a life whatever, the subject's own account included.

Consider a woman who, asked why she became a physician, describes a hospital ward in which she sat for three weeks at the age of nine. She did not sit there in order to become a physician. Thousands of children have sat in such wards and gone into other work. The selection is retrospective, the ordering is retrospective, and the ward has acquired a meaning it did not have while she was inside it. Yet nobody says that she has falsified her life. We say that she has understood it, or at least that she has made a serious attempt on it.

Pressed consistently, then, the objection condemns self-understanding along with biography, and that is a higher price than the objection is worth. But a complaint can be wrong in its conclusion and right about what it noticed, and something here is worth keeping. It is a distinction between two kinds of retrospection, one of which stays answerable to what is known of the episode and one of which does not. A biographer who turns the ward into a vocation must still show us the ward.

On this account the failure of bad biography is not shape but the concealment of shape. The offending books do not arrange a life; every book does that, and a book that did not would be a chronology. They present the arrangement as discovered rather than made, so that the reader is handed an interpretation written in the grammar of a finding. Nothing whatever prevents a writer from saying plainly that a life comes with no plot, and then offering one, and defending it.

The hardest case for my position is a life that resists. Some people's decades show no development; the late work is no advance on the early; the turning points were other people's decisions. Here the demand for narrative becomes coercive, because any shape at all will be more shapely than the life was. I do not conclude that such lives should go unwritten. I conclude that their biographies have to be built so that the refusal is visible, with episodes set beside one another and the connections between them left unasserted, so that no reader is handed a development that nobody lived. Books of that kind are seldom read with pleasure. That is a fact about readers, and not an argument about lives.

A census looks like an exercise in counting, and its categories look like the containers that counting requires. Before enumerators can report how many people live in a country, somebody must decide what kinds of people there are to be reported, and the deciding appears to be the dull preliminary to the interesting number. The history of the instrument suggests a different relation. Several categories that now seem to name obvious facts about a population were produced by the administrative needs of particular censuses, and went on to organize the way the counted population described itself.

The occupational classification is the clearest case. Early modern tax and parish registers recorded what a man was called in his own community, in a style that mixed trade, status and position in a household, so that one entry read as a craft and the next as a rank. Nineteenth-century statistical offices needed figures that could be added together across districts, and so built schedules of mutually exclusive occupations, with each person to be assigned exactly one. The schedules had effects the offices did not intend. A woman who kept the accounts of a workshop and also kept its household was recorded under one heading or under none, and the resulting tables showed a labour force more male than the workshops were.

The movement from category to self-description is the part that is easy to miss, and the part that matters. Census forms are filled in by the people they describe, and a form teaches. Once a schedule offers a fixed list, those filling it in learn which of their circumstances are legible to the state and which must be made to fit. Work on household schedules in several countries finds that the share of returns naming a single head of household rose sharply in the decades after that line was added to the form, in populations whose living arrangements were changing far more slowly.

It would be easy to overstate this, and the objection that the whole argument confuses measurement with reality deserves a direct answer. A census category is not a magic word. It does not bring a group into existence, and the people recorded under one heading or another go on living as they did. The answer is that the categories do not create the underlying circumstances but do redistribute the attention and the money that follow from counting. A ministry allocating school places works from tables, not from households. A group that appears in no cell of the table is not thereby abolished, but it is unfunded, and after several administrative generations the difference between the two is harder to see than it ought to be.

The same history cuts against a convenient conclusion, which is that better categories would end the difficulty. Every schedule must be finite in order to be countable, and every finite schedule will cut across somebody's circumstances. The recommendation that survives is modest and procedural. Statistical offices can publish the reasoning behind a schedule and the alternatives they rejected, and can break a series openly when a category changes rather than bridging it quietly, so that a later analyst can see which part of a change belongs to the population and which to the form.

Counting is therefore neither neutral in the way its defenders assume nor arbitrary in the way its critics imply. It is an administrative act with a history, and the history can be recovered from the schedules themselves.

I have spent fifteen years making the case for architectural preservation, and the evidence I assembled points somewhere I decline to go. The refusal is only interesting if the case is strong, so the case had better come first.

It runs like this. A street of old buildings carries information that cannot be reconstructed. The depth of a doorway, the width of a lot, the awkward angle where two builders met in the 1830s: each records a decision taken by somebody whose reasons are written down nowhere else. When a quarter is demolished and rebuilt faithfully, what comes back is a drawing of the quarter, accurate in every dimension and empty of the decisions that produced the dimensions. The loss runs one way only. Demolition takes a week and cannot be undone, while repair is slow and can always be done later. An asymmetry of that kind argues for a presumption against removal, and the presumption is not a sentimental one.

The conclusion the evidence invites is that the presumption should be close to absolute, and for some years I wrote as though it were. What stopped me was not a counterargument but a set of streets. In the quarters where preservation has worked best, the fabric is intact and nobody who lives there could have built it. The trades are gone, the lots cannot be subdivided, the uses are fixed by the same instruments that fixed the facades, and the only decisions still being taken concern paint. The buildings record a practice. The practice has stopped.

The point is not the familiar complaint that preservation raises rents, which is true and which other people have made better than I could. It is that the thing I claimed to value was a record of decisions, and a street where no further decisions may be taken has stopped keeping the record. Pressed to its limit, the argument for preservation destroys the property it was invoked to protect. I cannot see a way round that, and I have stopped looking for one.

A colleague answers that I have run two goods together. The record and the living practice are distinct, she says, and need not be housed in the same street: protect districts for the record, and let the practice work itself out elsewhere in the city. The answer is strong and I accept part of it. Some fabric is too fine to be subject to anybody's further decisions, and nothing is gained by pretending otherwise. As a general policy, though, the division fails, because a city's pressure to change does not fall evenly. It falls hardest where the streets are oldest, the plots smallest and the ground best served, which is to say in precisely the districts the policy would freeze. The practice is sent to the places where nothing much wants to happen.

What I now defend is not a presumption but a rate. A quarter should be expected to lose and replace some fraction of its fabric in each generation, and the policy question is the size of that fraction and who decides it, not whether the fraction is zero. A city that changes nothing and a city that changes everything fail in the same way, because both stop recording. I should say plainly that the rate cannot be derived from the evidence I began with. The evidence establishes what is lost by removal and says nothing about what is lost by stillness, which I had to learn from the streets.

The complaint that the national accounts leave out what matters is old and, in its usual form, unanswerable. Unpaid work in a household goes unrecorded. A fishery being emptied enters the accounts as income. A flood that destroys a town raises measured output while the town is rebuilt. The complaint is generally taken to support a single conclusion, that the headline aggregate should be replaced. It supports two conclusions, which the first generation of critics ran together and which call for different remedies.

The first is a claim about the production boundary. The accounts record what passes through a market or can be assigned a defensible market price, which leaves outside the boundary the care of children by their parents, the maintenance of a house by the people in it, and the unpaid labour of neighbours and volunteers. Time-use surveys in a number of countries put the hours involved at a magnitude comparable to recorded employment. Nothing in the theory of the accounts forbids counting these hours; the obstacles are the cost of the surveys and the conventions of the offices that run them, and satellite accounts that estimate household production already exist where an office has chosen to build one. This is a boundary problem, and boundary problems have technical remedies.

The second claim is of another kind. Output is a flow, measured over a period. A fishery, a forest, a stock of skills, a settled climate are stocks. A flow measure will register the drawing-down of a stock as activity, because from inside a single period that is what drawing it down looks like. Widening the boundary does nothing about this. One could count every hour of unpaid care in the country and still record the liquidation of a forest as a good year.

Running the two claims together produced a generation of proposals that cannot do what they promise: a single corrected aggregate, from which an estimate of depletion has been subtracted, offered as the figure that answers the critics. The arithmetic is unobjectionable and the result is a number that answers the boundary complaint while concealing the stock complaint, because once depletion has been folded into a flow it can be offset by activity elsewhere. A country that fells its forests and expands its restaurants reports a good year, and the arrangement that was built to prevent this reports it too.

Defenders of a single figure make a political argument that deserves to be taken seriously. A dashboard of indicators is a dashboard nobody reads; a government required to announce several numbers will announce whichever one is favourable, and a public that must weigh seven series against each other will attend to none of them. The cost is real and I do not think it can be argued away. But the remedy for selective announcement is a published rule about which figures are released together, and on what dates, rather than the pretence that one figure can carry two kinds of information.

Separating the claims clarifies what to ask of a statistical office. Widen the boundary wherever an imputation can be defended, and report stocks as stocks, on their own schedule, in their own units: tonnes of fish, hectares of forest, years of schooling. Neither reform waits on the other. The second is the one the accounts as presently constructed cannot be persuaded to do, and it is the one the critics most often trade away in exchange for a corrected headline number.

Disputes about the canon are conducted as though the question were which books deserve a place on the list. I want to ask the prior question: how a list comes to have the kind of authority that makes deserving the relevant idea at all. The most useful comparison I know is the common law.

A judge deciding a case does not consult a code that settles it. She consults earlier decisions, whose authority rests not on anyone having decreed them correct but on their having been relied upon. A decision followed for a century governs; a decision distinguished often enough stops governing without ever being overruled; and no official act marks either change. A reading list works the same way. Nothing was promulgated. Books acquire standing by being taught, cited, imitated, quarrelled with, and set up as the thing a new book has to get past. Nothing was ever voted on, and nothing is removed by a vote either: a book leaves the list by ceasing to be what other work has to answer.

The comparison explains several features of the dispute that the dispute itself cannot explain. It explains why there is no authoritative copy of the canon and never has been, and why the attempts to print one read as oddly presumptuous. It explains why additions are slow and why they are irreversible once made. It explains why both parties feel genuinely wronged: those who find the list closed against them and those who find it dissolving are describing the same institution, one in which nobody is in charge and therefore nobody can be petitioned. And it explains why direct argument that a book has been underrated so rarely works, while anything that obliges other writers to deal with the book works quite well.

An analogy earns its keep by being pushed until it breaks, and this one breaks at a particular joint. The authority of precedent is held in place by a duty. A judge must decide the case in front of her, must give reasons, and must treat like cases alike; reliance is not optional, and a judge who ignored the decisions on point would be reversed. There is no case in front of the reader. Nobody is obliged to read anything, no reasons need be given for not reading it, and no tribunal reviews the omission. Whatever makes a canon, it is not the discipline of having to decide.

That difference matters for practice, and it cuts against the party I am the more sympathetic to. If standing arises from reliance and nothing compels reliance, then exhortation does less than its authors hope: the published list of neglected books, the essay urging that a writer be read, the prize awarded to repair a reputation. What does the work is whatever manufactures an obligation to engage. A syllabus, an examination, an edition cheap enough to assign to thirty students, a translation good enough to argue with: these create the case in front of the reader that the analogy says is otherwise missing.

It cuts the other way too. Nothing in the arrangement makes an inherited list the residue of accumulated judgement rather than accumulated convenience. Reliance records what was available, assigned, in print and in a language the assigners read, which is not the same as what was best. So the honest description is uncomfortable for everyone holding a position in the quarrel. A canon is a record of what has had to be answered, and a list that nobody is obliged to answer stays inert however loudly it is published.

When a technical dispute becomes public, it is conducted as a quarrel about evidence. A new treatment plant, a transmission line, a compound in a consumer product: one side produces studies, and the other produces studies, or produces doubts about the first set. Survey work on such episodes repeatedly turns up something this framing cannot accommodate. The two sides often agree about the quantity in dispute. Asked for a numerical estimate of the risk, residents who oppose a facility and officials who have approved it give figures that overlap substantially, and each group, shown the other's estimate, tends to call it plausible.

If the parties agree about the number, the disagreement is about something else, and the instruments that go on to ask about consequences locate it. Respondents differ sharply, and consistently, on two further items: who will bear the cost if the estimate turns out to be wrong, and who will decide whether it was wrong. In study after study, the opponents of a facility are the respondents who answer both questions with somebody other than themselves.

On this reading, what presents itself as a dispute about risk is a dispute about the distribution of error. The relabelling earns its keep because the two readings predict different things. If the quarrel were about evidence, more and better evidence would reduce it. Communication trials that supplied residents with additional technical material report movement in measures of stated knowledge and little movement in measures of stated opposition. Where trials instead included a binding mechanism, such as an independent monitor chosen with the residents or a compensation schedule triggered automatically by a measured exceedance, reported willingness to accept the facility moved further, with no new evidence introduced at all.

Two objections are serious. The first is that the agreement on numbers is an artefact of asking people for numbers, since a respondent with no estimate will anchor on whatever figure the question implies. This is testable and has been tested: the overlap survives when the item is put as a frequency, as a comparison with a familiar hazard, or as a choice between described outcomes. The second objection is that the binding mechanisms work by paying people to accept a risk they continue to regard as unjustified, which makes the result a settlement rather than an agreement. I think that objection is correct, and it is a reason to describe the mechanisms accurately rather than to abandon them.

What the relocation does not license is the conclusion now fashionable in both directions, that expertise is therefore beside the point. The estimates in these episodes were produced by technical work, both parties use them, and the overlap between the two sides exists because the work was done. The finding is narrower than that. A credential confers standing on the first question and none at all on the second. Who should carry the cost of a mistake is not a technical question, and an expert who answers it is answering outside the competence that the public has any means of checking.

This suggests that measured trust in institutions is less a judgement about competence than an answer to a question about exposure. It would explain a pattern that the competence account finds awkward, namely that bodies with unblemished records are distrusted most reliably by the people who would carry the error if a record were broken.

Systems for notating dance are usually discussed as failures of a familiar kind. A score can fix where a limb goes and when it goes there; it cannot fix the quality of the going, and quality, everyone agrees, is where the dance lives. From this comes the standard position: the knowledge of a dance is held in trained bodies, passed from body to body in a studio, and a score is at best an aid to memory for somebody who already knows the work.
I hold a version of that position myself, and I think the strong version, which is the one usually stated, has to account for a case it cannot describe.

A work set down in notation in the 1930s and not performed for forty years was reconstructed from the score alone, by dancers who had never seen it and whose company included no one who had. The reconstruction was difficult and took a season. It was also successful by the only test available: those who had seen the original pronounced it recognizable, and in several passages better documented than their own recollections, which disagreed with one another about the order of two sections. On the strong view this should not have happened, because on the strong view the score cannot carry a work to anyone who does not already have it. The difficulty is not that the strong view underestimates notation. It is that the strong view has no description of what those dancers were doing.

What the case forces is a distinction between two things a score was supposed to supply and does not supply equally. One is the work's identity: what has to happen for this to be that dance and not another, including the sequence, the counts, the spatial design, the relation of one body to the next. The other is its manner: the weight of an arm as it falls, where in a phrase the breath goes, how much of a gesture is given to the audience. The score carried identity and did not carry manner. The reconstruction worked because identity is what a revival needs from the past, and manner is what a company can supply out of its own training.

A defender of the strong view replies that the revival succeeded only because the tradition had not in fact been broken: the reconstructors were trained in a technique descended from the one the work was made in, and they read the score with bodies that already knew how such a phrase should fall. That reply is right, and it limits my conclusion instead of refuting it. A score is not self-sufficient. It is an instruction addressed to a practice, and in a company with an unrelated technique it would yield something unrecognizable. But an instruction addressed to a practice is a long way from an aid to memory for somebody who already knows the work, which is the claim at issue.

The useful consequence concerns what to keep. A company that notates diligently while allowing its technique to lapse ends with a set of instructions nobody can read. A company that maintains its technique and notates nothing keeps the ability to perform work it can no longer identify, which is how repertory quietly becomes new choreography. The two records are not substitutes for one another, and the long argument about which of them is the real repository of dance has been an argument about a false alternative.

The standard working day is usually explained by the thing it is named after. Workers wanted fewer hours, organized to demand them, and legislation eventually fixed them: demand, agitation, statute, in that order. The records of inspection and of the campaigns themselves, read in sequence, suggest that the explanation has the direction of causation partly reversed. In several industries a standard day was already in place before the relevant statute, and what the statute did was not to shorten the day but to make it uniform across the trades that had not managed to produce one.

The returns of factory inspectors in the decades before the general statutes show a distribution of daily hours that was already clustering. Firms in the same trade and the same town converged on a common day well before any law required it, and the convergence followed the installation of machinery whose running time had to be coordinated across a whole shop. A single engine turning a single line shaft does not permit staggered arrivals. Belts are thrown on or they are not, and where the shaft turned, the day was the same length for everybody attached to it.

What the technology produced was standardization, not shortening, and the two have been run together because they arrived in the same decades. Hours worked under a shaft were often very long. What changed was that they became collective. A worker could no longer trade an hour for a few extra pence on her own account, because her hour was no longer hers to trade; it belonged to the shop. The campaigns for a shorter day are on this reading partly an effect of that collectivization rather than its cause, since a demand for fewer hours becomes a demand that can be pressed only once hours are something a whole shop holds in common.

The obvious objection is that demands for a shorter day are older than the machinery. This is correct. Petitions for a ten-hour day survive from trades that had no engine and no shaft, and from decades before either existed. So the claim cannot be that collectivization created the demand. The claim is about what made the demand effective. A scattered grievance became a bargaining position when the thing demanded could be granted only to everybody at once, so that no individual worker could be induced to break ranks by the offer of an extra hour's pay. Indivisibility is what gave the demand its leverage, and indivisibility came from the machinery.

That reading makes a prediction, and the prediction can be checked against trades the machinery never reorganized in this way. In home work, in dock work paid by the ship, and in trades paid by the piece, the standard day arrived late, arrived by statute rather than by agreement, and was evaded extensively for a generation afterwards. In those trades the sequence really was demand, agitation, statute, and it is where the sequence worked least well.

None of this makes the statutes unimportant, and it would be a poor history that treated them as ratification. They extended a standard to the trades that could not generate one, made a norm enforceable against the employer who would otherwise undercut his competitors, and in time shortened what they had first made uniform. But a norm is far easier to enforce than to invent. The standard day was invented, in the industries that had it first, by a machine's requirement that everybody start together.

Every attempt to define the essay by something it contains has failed, and the failures are instructive enough to be worth running through in order. Something does survive them, but what survives is a negative.

The first candidate is subject matter. The essay, it is said, takes up whatever is at hand and treats it without ceremony: a window, an illness, a quarrel overheard on a train. So does the newspaper column, and so does the sermon, and nobody confuses the three. The second candidate is length. Here the proposals are at least precise, and they are refuted with embarrassing ease, since no boundary anyone has drawn survives a famous counterexample at either end. There are essays of two pages and essays that fill a volume, and the volume is not a book of essays.

The third candidate is the first person. An essay is supposed to be the record of a particular mind, present on the page and declining to hide. But there are essays written throughout in the third person that nobody would call anything else, and there are memoirs saturated with the first person that are not essays and were not meant to be. Presence on the page is a tendency of the form, not a condition of it.

The fourth candidate is the best, and it is the reason the question is usually treated as settled. The essay, on this account, thinks in public: it exhibits the process of arriving rather than the result, and that process is the form. This is nearly right, which is why it persuades. But a laboratory notebook also exhibits a process of arriving, and the resemblance breaks exactly where it matters. The notebook's process is answerable to a question posed before the work began, and a notebook that wandered into another subject would be a bad notebook. The essayist's question is permitted to change under him, and an essay that ends somewhere other than where it set out is not thereby defective. What the fourth candidate describes is not a method. It is a permission.

What the four failures have in common is that each looks for something the essay does, and what marks the form off is a set of things it declines to do. It declines to establish. It declines to settle its question before beginning. It declines the obligation to be of use by the end. An essay that has proved its point has become an argument; one that knew its conclusion on the first page has become an exposition; one that must leave the reader better equipped has become advice. Each of those is a respectable form with standards of its own, and the essay is what is left when the obligations that constitute them are suspended.

The natural complaint is that this makes the essay parasitic: a form defined by exemptions from duties other forms accept, and therefore incapable of being done well or badly except by borrowed standards. The complaint would hold if the refusals were mere abstentions. But a refusal can be executed well or badly, and readers judge them so without any difficulty. We convict an essay of having known its conclusion from the first sentence, of having argued where it should have looked, of having closed in a maxim because it could not bear to close in a difficulty. Those are not borrowed standards. They belong to a form whose discipline is to hold a question open longer than is comfortable, which is harder than it sounds and is the only thing the essay has ever been for.

questions.stem: The author's main point about the retrospective shaping of a life is that it:

choices.A: is a distortion that the most careful biographers manage to avoid
choices.B: makes the biography of an undeveloped life impossible to write
choices.C: matters less than whether the episodes a biographer selects are accurate
choices.D: belongs to any account of a life, the subject's own account included

questions.explanation: The second paragraph states the point in those terms: retrospective conferral is 'not the peculiar vice of biographers but the condition of any account of a life whatever, the subject's own account included'. The whole argument is built on that parity.

wrong.A: The author grants that the shaping is unavoidable rather than treating it as a lapse that skill could prevent.
wrong.B: The sixth paragraph says the opposite about resistant lives: 'I do not conclude that such lives should go unwritten.'
wrong.C: Answerability to what is known of an episode is one of the author's conditions, but it is introduced as a refinement, not as the claim the passage is built toward.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of the standard complaint against biography is best described as:

choices.A: rejecting its premise while accepting the conclusion drawn from it
choices.B: showing that its evidence was gathered from unrepresentative books
choices.C: tracing it to the period in which biography became a popular form
choices.D: accepting its premise and denying the conclusion drawn from it

questions.explanation: The second paragraph announces the move: 'I propose to grant the premise without reservation', followed by 'The conclusion still does not follow.' The premise is conceded and the inference is refused.

wrong.A: This reverses the structure. The premise about retrospective significance is the part the author grants outright.
wrong.B: No books are surveyed. The argument turns on what any account of a life must do, not on a sample of biographies.
wrong.C: The passage offers no history of the form or of the complaint, and dates nothing.

questions.stem: The example of the woman who became a physician functions in the argument as:

choices.A: evidence that early experience governs the choice of an adult occupation
choices.B: an illustration of the kind of episode a biographer ought not to use
choices.C: a case in which retrospective selection is not counted as falsification
choices.D: a concession that some lives do carry a plot that can be discovered

questions.explanation: The paragraph grants that her selection and ordering are retrospective and then draws the contrast: 'Yet nobody says that she has falsified her life.' The example exists to show that we do not treat backward-looking selection as a lie when the subject does it.

wrong.A: The passage says the reverse about causation, noting that thousands of children 'have sat in such wards and gone into other work'.
wrong.B: The ward is the example of an episode a biographer may legitimately use, provided the biographer still shows us the ward.
wrong.D: Her story is retrospective construction, not a plot found in the life; the author elsewhere says a life 'comes with no plot'.

questions.stem: The distinction the author draws in the fifth paragraph implies that a biography is open to criticism when it:

choices.A: selects episodes that the subject herself would not have chosen
choices.B: supplies a shape for a life that was in fact lived without one
choices.C: presents its arrangement as something found rather than made
choices.D: declines to say which episodes were the subject's turning points

questions.explanation: The paragraph locates the fault precisely: the offending books 'present the arrangement as discovered rather than made'. What is criticized is the concealment of shape, not shape.

wrong.A: The author's own example has the subject and the biographer doing the same kind of selecting, so divergence between them is not the fault identified.
wrong.B: This is what the author says every book does, adding that a book which did not would be a chronology.
wrong.D: Leaving connections unasserted is recommended in the final paragraph for resistant lives, not treated as a defect.

questions.stem: The author's argument would be most weakened by evidence that:

choices.A: readers of biography strongly prefer books with a clear narrative shape
choices.B: biographers disagree about which episodes of a famous life matter most
choices.C: most people's accounts of their own lives change over several decades
choices.D: people asked about their choices describe them without reference to an outcome

questions.explanation: Everything turns on the parity claimed in the second paragraph, that the subject's own account is retrospective too. If self-accounts were not organized around an ending already in hand, biography's shaping would be its peculiar vice after all, which is exactly the conclusion the author denies.

wrong.A: A preference among readers bears on what sells, and the author already grants that the recommended books are 'seldom read with pleasure'.
wrong.B: Disagreement among biographers is consistent with the author's view, on which arrangement is made rather than found.
wrong.C: Changing self-accounts support the author, since they show significance being conferred afresh from later vantage points.

questions.stem: A biographer takes on a composer whose works show no stylistic progression and whose commissions were all arranged by a patron. The author would most likely recommend that she:

choices.A: organize the book around the patron, who supplied what development there was
choices.B: set the episodes beside one another and leave their connections unclaimed
choices.C: decline the subject, since such a life cannot be honestly narrated
choices.D: look harder for the pattern, since a patient reader finds one in any life

questions.explanation: This is the resistant life of the final paragraph, where turning points 'were other people's decisions'. The remedy given there is a book built 'with episodes set beside one another and the connections between them left unasserted'.

wrong.A: Supplying a development the composer did not live is the coercion the paragraph warns against; the patron's decisions are part of what makes the life resistant.
wrong.C: The author states directly that he does not conclude that such lives should go unwritten.
wrong.D: The passage denies that lives come with patterns waiting to be found, and says any shape here 'will be more shapely than the life was'.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: showing that census figures are too unreliable for administrative use
choices.B: the difficulty of counting people who move between several households
choices.C: how census categories arose and what their use does to the counted
choices.D: the case for abandoning fixed schedules in official statistics

questions.explanation: The first paragraph sets out both halves of the subject: categories 'were produced by the administrative needs of particular censuses, and went on to organize the way the counted population described itself'. The paragraphs that follow supply the origin and then the effect.

wrong.A: The author treats the tables as consequential rather than useless, noting that a ministry allocating school places works from them.
wrong.B: Household composition appears as one example in the third paragraph, not as the subject of the passage.
wrong.D: The final recommendation keeps the schedules and asks only that offices publish their reasoning and break series openly.

questions.stem: According to the passage, nineteenth-century statistical offices built schedules of mutually exclusive occupations because they needed figures that:

choices.A: matched the descriptions people used in their own communities
choices.B: could be compared with the earlier tax and parish registers
choices.C: could be added together across districts
choices.D: kept a person's trade distinct from a person's rank

questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives the reason directly: the offices 'needed figures that could be added together across districts, and so built schedules of mutually exclusive occupations'.

wrong.A: That is the older practice the schedules replaced, and the passage says those descriptions could not be added up.
wrong.B: Comparison with the registers is nowhere given as a motive; the registers appear only as the style of record that preceded the schedules.
wrong.D: Separating trade from rank is a feature of the new schedules rather than the need that produced them.

questions.stem: The rise in returns naming a single head of household is presented as evidence that:

choices.A: the list of choices on a form shapes how respondents describe themselves
choices.B: living arrangements changed faster in that period than had been thought
choices.C: respondents misreport their circumstances when categories are unfamiliar
choices.D: households with one head became more common once they were counted

questions.explanation: The finding is introduced to illustrate the claim that 'a form teaches': the share of such returns rose 'in populations whose living arrangements were changing far more slowly', so what moved was the description and not the arrangement.

wrong.B: The passage says the arrangements changed far more slowly than the returns did, which is the whole force of the example.
wrong.C: Nothing is said about error. The point is that respondents learn which circumstances the form can register.
wrong.D: This reads the change as happening in the households rather than in their self-description, which is the confusion the passage is warning against.

questions.stem:
The passage supports which of the following statements about the objection that the argument confuses measurement with reality?

I. The author considers it serious enough to answer directly
II. The author grants that categories do not create the circumstances they record
III. The author replies that the difference between being uncounted and not existing is merely verbal

choices.A: I only
choices.B: I and II only
choices.C: I and III only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the objection 'deserves a direct answer', which settles I, and concedes that the categories 'do not create the underlying circumstances', which settles II.

wrong.A: This drops the explicit concession that a census category 'is not a magic word' and does not bring a group into existence.
wrong.C: Statement III overstates the author, who says only that after several administrative generations the difference is 'harder to see than it ought to be'.
wrong.D: Statements I and II hold, but III turns a remark about how the difference becomes obscured into a claim that there is no difference.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about redistributed resources?

choices.A: Districts whose common household form had no line on the schedule received fewer school places than their numbers warranted
choices.B: Ministries in several countries now draw household data from registers rather than from the census
choices.C: Occupational tables from the nineteenth century have since been recompiled by historians on better definitions
choices.D: Respondents who find no suitable category on a form commonly leave the item blank

questions.explanation: The claim is that a group absent from the table 'is unfunded', with the school-places example given as the mechanism. Choice A reports exactly that allocation gap and connects it to the missing line on the schedule.

wrong.B: A later change of data source says nothing about whether the counting affected allocation when the census was the source.
wrong.C: Recompiling old tables bears on historical scholarship, not on the money and attention that followed from the original counts.
wrong.D: Blank items explain how people fall out of the tables, which the author already asserts; the disputed step is the consequence for resources.

questions.stem: The author would most likely regard a proposal to replace the present occupational schedule with a much longer and finer one as:

choices.A: promising, since the chief defect of a schedule is its coarseness
choices.B: pointless, since respondents adapt their answers to whatever list they are given
choices.C: harmful, since a longer list would break comparison with earlier series
choices.D: insufficient, since any countable list still cuts across some circumstances

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph rejects the hope that better categories would end the difficulty: 'Every schedule must be finite in order to be countable, and every finite schedule will cut across somebody's circumstances.'

wrong.A: The passage denies that refinement is the remedy, which is why its recommendation is procedural rather than a better list.
wrong.B: Adaptation is why schedules matter on this account, not a reason to leave one unchanged; the author asks for published reasoning, not inaction.
wrong.C: The author accepts breaks in a series and asks only that they be made openly rather than bridged quietly.

questions.stem: The author's central claim is that a quarter of a city should:

choices.A: be governed by whichever instruments its residents prefer
choices.B: replace a limited share of its fabric in each generation
choices.C: be rebuilt faithfully where the original fabric is beyond repair
choices.D: be protected from the rent increases that preservation brings

questions.explanation: The final paragraph states the position: 'A quarter should be expected to lose and replace some fraction of its fabric in each generation', and the open question is the size of the fraction rather than whether it is zero.

wrong.A: Who decides the rate is named as an open question, not settled in favour of residents.
wrong.C: Faithful rebuilding is the author's example of what fails, returning 'a drawing of the quarter' emptied of the decisions behind it.
wrong.D: The rent complaint is explicitly set aside as not the author's point, though he grants it is true.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what a faithful rebuilding fails to bring back is:

choices.A: the accuracy of the quarter's original dimensions
choices.B: the information that drawings and surveys preserve
choices.C: the quarter's usefulness to the people who live there
choices.D: the decisions whose traces the original fabric held

questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the rebuilt quarter is 'accurate in every dimension and empty of the decisions that produced the dimensions', and the preceding sentences identify those decisions as what the old fabric records.

wrong.A: Dimensional accuracy is precisely what the author grants a faithful rebuilding achieves.
wrong.B: Drawings are the author's figure for what survives rebuilding, not for what is lost.
wrong.C: Usefulness to residents is not the measure the passage applies to rebuilding.

questions.stem: The author describes the well-preserved quarters whose residents could not have built them in order to:

choices.A: argue that preservation policy is usually administered incompetently
choices.B: concede that the evidence for preservation is weaker than he claimed
choices.C: show that fabric can survive while the practice behind it does not
choices.D: explain why rebuilding is cheaper than continuous repair

questions.explanation: The third paragraph ends on exactly that contrast: 'The buildings record a practice. The practice has stopped.'

wrong.A: These are the quarters 'where preservation has worked best', so the example is not one of maladministration.
wrong.B: The author insists the case for preservation is strong and says the refusal is interesting only because it is.
wrong.D: Relative cost is used in the second paragraph to argue for a presumption against removal, not to explain these streets.

questions.stem: The author's response to the colleague who separates the record from the living practice is best described as:

choices.A: a rejection, on the ground that the two goods cannot be told apart
choices.B: a partial acceptance, limited by where a city's pressure to change falls
choices.C: an acceptance, together with a proposal to enlarge the protected districts
choices.D: a refusal to answer, on the ground that the distinction is merely verbal

questions.explanation: He writes 'The answer is strong and I accept part of it', then limits it: 'a city's pressure to change does not fall evenly' and falls hardest in the districts the policy would freeze.

wrong.A: He treats the two as distinguishable and concedes that some fabric should indeed be removed from further decisions.
wrong.C: Enlarging the protected districts would worsen the problem he identifies, since those districts are where change is most wanted.
wrong.D: He answers the distinction at length rather than dismissing it.

questions.stem: All of the following are consistent with the author's position EXCEPT:

choices.A: a building of exceptional quality is placed beyond further alteration
choices.B: a quarter that has replaced nothing in a century is failing his test
choices.C: a city that rebuilds its centre entirely keeps the better record
choices.D: the right rate of replacement cannot be read off the evidence for preservation

questions.explanation: The final paragraph rules this out: 'A city that changes nothing and a city that changes everything fail in the same way, because both stop recording.'

wrong.A: He grants this directly, allowing that some fabric is too fine to be subject to anybody's further decisions.
wrong.B: Stillness is the failure he spent the passage establishing, so a quarter at a rate of zero fails his test.
wrong.D: He says so himself, adding that the evidence 'says nothing about what is lost by stillness'.

questions.stem: A city freezes one old quarter completely and permits unrestricted rebuilding in the quarter next to it. The author would most likely object that:

choices.A: neither quarter will go on recording the decisions he values
choices.B: the frozen quarter will lose its residents to the rebuilt one
choices.C: the policy keeps the record and the practice in one street
choices.D: the rate of replacement next door will be impossible to measure

questions.explanation: The arrangement produces one quarter at a rate of zero and one at a rate of everything, and the passage says both failures are the same failure: 'both stop recording'.

wrong.B: Population movement is not the author's criterion; he sets aside the rent and residency complaints as other people's arguments.
wrong.C: The policy does the reverse, separating the two into different quarters, which is the colleague's proposal.
wrong.D: Measurement is not raised as a difficulty anywhere in the passage; what is open is the size of the fraction and who sets it.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that the headline growth aggregate should be replaced by a dashboard
choices.B: show that unpaid household work exceeds the value of recorded employment
choices.C: defend the national accounts against the complaint that they omit what matters
choices.D: distinguish two complaints about the accounts that need different remedies

questions.explanation: The first paragraph announces the structure: the complaint 'supports two conclusions, which the first generation of critics ran together and which call for different remedies', and the rest of the passage separates them.

wrong.A: A dashboard is treated as having a real cost, and the author's remedy is a published release rule rather than a replacement aggregate.
wrong.B: The passage says only that time-use surveys put the hours at a magnitude comparable to recorded employment.
wrong.C: The author grants the complaint and calls it unanswerable in its usual form; the dispute is over what follows from it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the second of the two claims the author separates?

choices.A: An aggregate of flows cannot represent the condition of a stock
choices.B: The accounts record only what passes through a market
choices.C: Governments announce whichever figure happens to suit them
choices.D: Estimates of depletion are too uncertain to be subtracted

questions.explanation: The third paragraph sets out this claim: output 'is a flow, measured over a period' while fisheries, forests and skills are stocks, and 'a flow measure will register the drawing-down of a stock as activity'.

wrong.B: That is the first claim, about the production boundary, which the author says has a technical remedy.
wrong.C: This is the political argument made by defenders of a single figure, not one of the two complaints.
wrong.D: The author calls the arithmetic of such subtractions 'unobjectionable'; his objection is to what the resulting number conceals.

questions.stem: The author objects to a corrected aggregate that subtracts an estimate of depletion because such a figure:

choices.A: rests on imputations that no statistical office can defend
choices.B: requires time-use data that most countries do not collect
choices.C: would be published only in years when the adjustment was small
choices.D: allows activity elsewhere to offset the loss of a stock

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph gives the reason: 'once depletion has been folded into a flow it can be offset by activity elsewhere', illustrated by the country that fells forests and expands restaurants.

wrong.A: Defensible imputation is something the author asks for in the final paragraph, and he raises no doubt about the arithmetic here.
wrong.B: Time-use data belongs to the boundary claim; the corrected aggregate he criticises concerns depletion of stocks.
wrong.C: Selective publication is the political argument of the fifth paragraph and is not his objection to this figure.

questions.stem: The author's handling of the political argument for a single figure is to:

choices.A: dismiss it as a defence of official convenience
choices.B: accept the cost it names and propose another remedy for it
choices.C: deny that governments choose among figures in the way described
choices.D: concede that it defeats the case for reporting stocks separately

questions.explanation: He writes that 'The cost is real and I do not think it can be argued away', and then offers a different remedy, 'a published rule about which figures are released together'.

wrong.A: He calls the argument one that 'deserves to be taken seriously' rather than treating it as self-serving.
wrong.C: He grants the behaviour, saying a government required to announce several numbers will announce the favourable one.
wrong.D: The final paragraph presses the separate reporting of stocks as the reform that matters most.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the boundary complaint has a technical remedy?

choices.A: No defensible method exists for assigning a value to an hour of unpaid care
choices.B: Time-use surveys are run far less often than the accounts are published
choices.C: Satellite accounts for household production exist in only a few countries
choices.D: Unpaid hours of care per household have fallen over recent decades

questions.explanation: The remedy depends on there being a price to impute: the accounts record what 'can be assigned a defensible market price', and the author asks offices to widen the boundary 'wherever an imputation can be defended'. If no such valuation is defensible, the technical fix is unavailable rather than merely expensive.

wrong.B: Infrequency is a question of cost and timing, which the author already names as the obstacle rather than a reason the remedy fails.
wrong.C: Scarcity of such accounts is consistent with the author, who says they exist 'where an office has chosen to build one'.
wrong.D: A falling quantity of unpaid care changes the size of the omission, not whether it can be counted.

questions.stem: A government announces that it will publish a quarterly growth figure and, separately each year, a report on the state of its fisheries, forests and water. The author would most likely regard this as:

choices.A: mistaken, since the two will be read as rival accounts of the same thing
choices.B: acceptable only if the fisheries report is converted into the units of the growth figure
choices.C: the right shape, since stocks are then reported as stocks on their own schedule
choices.D: inadequate, because the growth figure still leaves out unpaid household work

questions.explanation: This is the recommendation of the final paragraph almost exactly: 'report stocks as stocks, on their own schedule, in their own units'.

wrong.A: The author wants the two kinds of information kept apart, and his worry about a single figure is that it merges them.
wrong.B: Conversion into the units of the flow figure is the move he rejects, since folding depletion into a flow allows it to be offset.
wrong.D: True of the boundary reform, but the passage insists that 'Neither reform waits on the other', so a report on stocks is not made inadequate by the boundary work still being undone.

questions.stem: The author's purpose in comparing a reading list to the common law is to:

choices.A: argue that literary standing ought to be settled by an authoritative body
choices.B: explain how books acquire standing without anybody conferring it
choices.C: show that judges and critics face the same kind of decision
choices.D: defend the inherited list as the residue of accumulated judgement

questions.explanation: The second paragraph draws the parallel precisely at this point: authority 'rests not on anyone having decreed them correct but on their having been relied upon', and on the list 'Nothing was promulgated.'

wrong.A: The passage treats the absence of anyone in charge as a fact about the institution, and calls attempts to print an authoritative list presumptuous.
wrong.C: The analogy is said to break at exactly this joint, since 'There is no case in front of the reader.'
wrong.D: The final paragraph denies this, noting that reliance records what was available and assigned.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a book loses its place on the list when:

choices.A: other work no longer has to answer it
choices.B: critics come to agree that it was overrated
choices.C: it goes out of print and is not reissued
choices.D: a rival book takes its place on syllabuses

questions.explanation: The second paragraph states it: 'a book leaves the list by ceasing to be what other work has to answer.'

wrong.B: The passage says nothing is removed by a vote, and that direct argument about a book's merit rarely moves its standing.
wrong.C: Cheap editions are named as one thing that creates an obligation to engage, but going out of print is not given as what removes a book.
wrong.D: Displacement by a rival is not the criterion; what matters is whether work still has to get past the book.

questions.stem: The author holds that the analogy with the common law breaks down because, unlike a judge, a reader:

choices.A: is not trained to give reasons for a judgement
choices.B: has no case that must be decided
choices.C: may rely on a book without ever citing it
choices.D: cannot tell a precedent from a binding rule

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph locates the joint: a judge 'must decide the case in front of her', while 'There is no case in front of the reader.'

wrong.A: Training is not the issue; the passage says no reasons need be given at all for not reading something.
wrong.C: Uncited reliance would fit the analogy rather than break it, since standing comes from being relied upon.
wrong.D: The reader's capacity to make distinctions is never in question in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the author regards the grievances of both parties to the canon dispute as:

choices.A: exaggerated, since the list in fact changes very little either way
choices.B: beside the point, since standing is not conferred by anyone's complaint
choices.C: evidence that the real quarrel is about syllabuses and examinations
choices.D: accurate reports of an institution that nobody administers

questions.explanation: The third paragraph says both parties 'feel genuinely wronged' and are 'describing the same institution, one in which nobody is in charge and therefore nobody can be petitioned'.

wrong.A: The author says additions are slow but also irreversible, and he does not accuse either party of exaggeration.
wrong.B: He treats the grievances as accurate descriptions rather than as irrelevancies.
wrong.C: Syllabuses appear later as the instruments that create obligation, not as the hidden subject of the dispute.

questions.stem:
On the basis of the passage, which of the following would be expected to raise a neglected book's standing?

I. Setting the book as required reading in an examined course
II. Publishing a widely circulated list that names the book as neglected
III. Showing that earlier readers of the book misjudged its merits

choices.A: I only
choices.B: I and II only
choices.C: I and III only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph names the effective instruments as those that manufacture 'an obligation to engage', beginning with 'A syllabus, an examination'. It explicitly discounts II, since 'the published list of neglected books' is among the exhortations that do 'less than its authors hope', and the third paragraph discounts III, since direct argument about merit 'so rarely works'.

wrong.B: The published list of neglected books is the author's own example of exhortation that disappoints.
wrong.C: An argument about earlier misjudgement is direct argument about merit, which the third paragraph says rarely moves standing.
wrong.D: Only the examined course creates the obligation the passage identifies as doing the work.

questions.stem: A critic argues that the inherited list must be nearly correct because it is what survived two centuries of informed choice. The author would most likely reply that:

choices.A: two centuries is too short a period for reliance to accumulate
choices.B: reliance records what was available and assigned as much as what was best
choices.C: the list is correct only for the readers who happened to produce it
choices.D: informed choice plays no part in whether a book is relied upon

questions.explanation: The final paragraph answers this argument in advance: reliance 'records what was available, assigned, in print and in a language the assigners read, which is not the same as what was best'.

wrong.A: No claim about how long accumulation takes is made; the author says additions are slow but offers no threshold.
wrong.C: This relativizes the list's merit, which goes further than the passage, and the author's point is about availability rather than about whose list it is.
wrong.D: Too strong. The author denies that the list is only judgement, not that judgement enters at all.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that public technical disputes are:

choices.A: disagreements about who bears the cost of a mistake rather than about estimates
choices.B: evidence that people without training misjudge the size of unfamiliar risks
choices.C: resolved once residents have been supplied with enough technical material
choices.D: a sign that technical expertise has lost its standing with the public

questions.explanation: The third paragraph states it: 'what presents itself as a dispute about risk is a dispute about the distribution of error', and the second paragraph identifies the two items on which the parties actually differ.

wrong.B: The survey evidence reported is that the two sides' estimates overlap, which cuts against any misjudgement account.
wrong.C: The communication trials found movement in stated knowledge and little in stated opposition.
wrong.D: The fifth paragraph rejects this conclusion directly, noting that the overlap 'exists because the work was done'.

questions.stem: The passage attributes all of the following to survey or trial evidence EXCEPT that:

choices.A: opponents and officials give overlapping numerical estimates of a risk
choices.B: extra technical material moved stated knowledge more than stated opposition
choices.C: monitoring and compensation arrangements moved stated willingness to accept
choices.D: residents offered compensation come to regard the risk as justified

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the opposite, accepting the objection that such mechanisms work 'by paying people to accept a risk they continue to regard as unjustified'. The other three are each reported as findings.

wrong.A: The first paragraph reports this overlap as the recurring survey result the usual framing cannot accommodate.
wrong.B: The third paragraph reports exactly this result from the communication trials.
wrong.C: The third paragraph reports that willingness moved further where a binding mechanism was included.

questions.stem: The author defends calling the quarrel a dispute about the distribution of error chiefly on the ground that the two readings:

choices.A: rest on different kinds of survey instrument
choices.B: assign different roles to technical credentials
choices.C: predict different results from supplying more evidence
choices.D: describe the opponents' motives in different terms

questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the relabelling 'earns its keep because the two readings predict different things', and the contrast drawn immediately after is between supplying evidence and installing a binding mechanism.

wrong.A: Both readings are tested with the same survey material; the instruments are how the question is settled, not what distinguishes the readings.
wrong.B: The role of credentials is a separate consequence taken up in the fifth paragraph, after the reading has been defended.
wrong.D: The passage reports what respondents say about cost and authority rather than attributing motives.

questions.stem: The author's response to the objection that the mechanisms pay people to accept an unjustified risk is to:

choices.A: agree with it and treat it as a reason to describe the mechanisms honestly
choices.B: reject it, since willingness to accept is what the trials set out to measure
choices.C: set it aside as a question that survey research cannot address
choices.D: answer that the residents' own estimates show the risk to be justified

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says so plainly: 'I think that objection is correct, and it is a reason to describe the mechanisms accurately rather than to abandon them.'

wrong.B: The author does not dispute the objection, and treating the measure as its own justification is not the move he makes.
wrong.C: He handles the first objection by reporting tests of it and the second by accepting it, not by declaring either out of reach.
wrong.D: Agreement on the estimate is not treated as settling whether the risk is justified, which is the second question the passage separates out.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most weaken the author's account of these disputes?

choices.A: Officials' estimates are produced by consultants whom the officials employ
choices.B: Compensation schedules are rarely triggered in the facilities that adopt them
choices.C: Residents who accept a facility later report low trust in its monitor
choices.D: Opposition falls as much when new studies are published as when a monitor is appointed

questions.explanation: The account rests on the differential prediction set out in the third paragraph, that evidence moves stated knowledge while a binding mechanism moves willingness. If publishing studies moved opposition as much as appointing a monitor, that contrast collapses.

wrong.A: Who paid for an estimate bears on its credibility, and the author's puzzle is that both sides nevertheless arrive at overlapping figures.
wrong.B: A schedule that is rarely triggered is consistent with the account, since what the residents gain is the allocation of the cost should an error occur.
wrong.C: Later distrust of a monitor says nothing about whether the dispute concerned the estimate or the distribution of error.

questions.stem: An engineer tells a public meeting that the community should accept the small measured risk from a plant. On the author's account she exceeds her competence because she is:

choices.A: applying an estimate from the laboratory to a setting nobody has studied
choices.B: answering a question about who should carry a possible error
choices.C: asserting a figure the residents have no means of checking
choices.D: treating a settlement as though it were an agreement

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph draws the line there: 'A credential confers standing on the first question and none at all on the second', and 'Who should carry the cost of a mistake is not a technical question.' Recommending acceptance answers that second question.

wrong.A: No mismatch between laboratory and setting is at issue; the passage grants that the estimates are sound technical work.
wrong.C: The passage reports that residents do produce and evaluate such figures, and what they cannot check is the expert's answer to the second question.
wrong.D: That description applies to the compensation mechanisms discussed in the fourth paragraph, not to a recommendation made at a meeting.

questions.stem: The author's main conclusion is that:

choices.A: a notated score can preserve a dance even where no practice survives
choices.B: notation and trained bodies preserve different things, and neither replaces the other
choices.C: the quality of a movement can be notated as precisely as its position
choices.D: the embodied account of dance knowledge is refuted by the revival described

questions.explanation: The final paragraph draws the conclusion: 'The two records are not substitutes for one another', after the fourth paragraph has separated identity, which the score carried, from manner, which the company supplied.

wrong.A: The author concedes the opposite, granting that a score 'is not self-sufficient' and would yield something unrecognizable in a company with an unrelated technique.
wrong.C: The passage accepts that a score cannot fix the quality of a movement, which is why manner has to come from training.
wrong.D: Too strong. The author says he holds a version of the embodied position himself, and that the defender's reply 'limits my conclusion instead of refuting it'.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that those who had seen the original work judged the reconstruction to be:

choices.A: accurate in its manner but not in its sequence of sections
choices.B: inferior to the record preserved in their own memories
choices.C: recognizable, and in places better documented than their recollections
choices.D: impossible to assess, since their recollections conflicted

questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that they 'pronounced it recognizable, and in several passages better documented than their own recollections'.

wrong.A: Sequence belongs to what the score carried; manner is what the score did not carry.
wrong.B: Their recollections are described as the weaker record, disagreeing about the order of two sections.
wrong.D: The conflict among their memories is given as part of why the reconstruction counted as successful, not as a reason judgement was unavailable.

questions.stem: The distinction between identity and manner serves in the argument to:

choices.A: concede that a score records nothing a dancer needs
choices.B: explain why witnesses to the original disagreed with each other
choices.C: show that the strong view is a claim about training rather than notation
choices.D: account for a revival that the strong view cannot describe

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens by saying the case 'forces' the distinction, and the case is the revival the previous paragraph says the strong view 'has no description of'.

wrong.A: The distinction does the reverse, isolating identity as the thing the score did carry.
wrong.B: The witnesses' disagreement is evidence about memory, and the distinction is not introduced to explain it.
wrong.C: Training enters later, in the defender's reply, and the author treats the strong view as a claim about what a score can transmit.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a company that notates its repertory while allowing its technique to lapse would end with:

choices.A: records that nobody in it can read
choices.B: manner preserved at the cost of identity
choices.C: the better of the two imperfect records
choices.D: the standard error made by the embodied view

questions.explanation: The final paragraph states the outcome: such a company 'ends with a set of instructions nobody can read', because a score is an instruction addressed to a practice.

wrong.B: It is manner that depends on living technique, so a lapsed technique loses manner and keeps the record of identity.
wrong.C: The passage refuses to rank the two records, calling the choice between them a false alternative.
wrong.D: The embodied view's error, on the author's telling, is to treat the score as a mere aid to memory, which is not what this company has done.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that a score is an instruction addressed to a practice?

choices.A: A revival from the same notation failed in a company trained in an unrelated technique
choices.B: A score prepared by a choreographer included extensive notes on breathing
choices.C: Dancers reconstructing a work consult film of other works by its choreographer
choices.D: Companies that perform a work continuously alter it gradually across decades

questions.explanation: The claim is stated with exactly this prediction attached: in a company with an unrelated technique a score 'would yield something unrecognizable'. A failure of that kind is the test the claim invites.

wrong.B: Notes on breathing would suggest a score can carry manner after all, which cuts against the division the author draws.
wrong.C: Consulting film shows reconstructors using additional sources, which bears on neither the score's dependence on a practice nor its carrying of identity.
wrong.D: Gradual drift in a continuously performed work supports the value of notation generally, without showing that a score needs a practice to be read.

questions.stem: A historian argues that since every revival depends on living technique, notation contributes nothing of its own. The author's position implies which reply?

choices.A: Technique varies too much between companies for a work to transmit at all
choices.B: Notation contributes the manner that a company's technique cannot supply
choices.C: Revivals built from notation are more faithful than revivals built from memory
choices.D: Without the score a company could still perform, but not know what it performed

questions.explanation: The final paragraph gives this reply directly: a company that notates nothing 'keeps the ability to perform work it can no longer identify'. Identity is the contribution the author assigns to notation.

wrong.A: The author relies on technique transmitting well enough to supply manner, so he cannot answer this way.
wrong.B: This inverts the division: manner is what training supplies and the score does not.
wrong.C: The passage compares what the two records preserve rather than ranking revivals by fidelity, and calls the ranking a false alternative.

questions.stem: The author's principal claim about the standard working day is that:

choices.A: mechanization made the day uniform before legislation made it shorter
choices.B: legislation was the decisive cause of both uniform and shorter hours
choices.C: the campaigns for shorter hours had no bearing on when the day arrived
choices.D: the standard day was adopted earliest in the trades paid by the piece

questions.explanation: The first paragraph states the reversal, that a standard day was in place before the statute and the statute made it uniform, and the last paragraph adds that the statutes 'in time shortened what they had first made uniform'.

wrong.B: This is the account the passage sets out to revise, with the order of causes partly reversed.
wrong.C: Too strong. The author grants the campaigns a role and asks only what made their demand effective.
wrong.D: Piece-rate trades are the author's example of where the standard day arrived late and was widely evaded.

questions.stem: The returns of factory inspectors are used to support the claim that:

choices.A: hours in mechanized shops were shorter than hours elsewhere
choices.B: inspectors were enforcing a standard day before the statutes existed
choices.C: wages in a single trade converged along with its hours
choices.D: firms in a trade settled on a common day without being required to

questions.explanation: The second paragraph reads the returns as showing hours 'already clustering', with firms in the same trade and town converging on a common day 'well before any law required it'.

wrong.A: The third paragraph says hours under a shaft were often very long, and that shortening is not what the technology produced.
wrong.B: The inspectors supply a record of practice; nothing is said about them enforcing a day no statute had set.
wrong.C: Pay appears only in the point about trading an hour for extra pence, and no claim about converging wages is made.

questions.stem: The author's concession about petitions from unmechanized trades leads him to restate his claim as one about:

choices.A: when the demand for shorter hours first arose
choices.B: what made the demand effective once it was made
choices.C: which trades the earliest statutes covered
choices.D: whether machinery lengthened or shortened the day

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph makes the restatement explicit: 'So the claim cannot be that collectivization created the demand. The claim is about what made the demand effective.'

wrong.A: That is the point he gives up, conceding that the petitions are older than the machinery.
wrong.C: Statutory coverage comes up in the final paragraph as something the statutes achieved, not as the restated claim.
wrong.D: He has already said that standardization rather than shortening is what the technology produced.

questions.stem: The author's reading predicts that in a trade where each worker's hours could be varied individually, a standard day would:

choices.A: arrive early and be closely observed
choices.B: arrive late and be poorly observed
choices.C: arrive by agreement rather than by statute
choices.D: arrive only where output was paced by a machine

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph tests the reading against exactly such trades, home work, dock work by the ship and piece-rate work, where the day 'arrived late, arrived by statute rather than by agreement, and was evaded extensively for a generation afterwards'.

wrong.A: Early arrival and close observance are what the reading predicts for the mechanized shops, where hours were indivisible.
wrong.C: Agreement is the route taken where the machinery had made hours collective; in these trades the day came by statute.
wrong.D: This denies that such trades ever got a standard day, whereas the passage says the statutes extended one to them.

questions.stem:
Based on the passage, the installation of a single engine driving every machine in a shop would be expected to bring about which of the following?

I. A common starting time for everyone attached to the shaft
II. A reduction in the number of hours worked each day
III. A loss of the individual worker's ability to sell an extra hour

choices.A: I only
choices.B: I and II only
choices.C: I and III only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives I, since a line shaft 'does not permit staggered arrivals', and the third gives III, since a worker 'could no longer trade an hour for a few extra pence on her own account'. The same paragraph denies II: hours under a shaft 'were often very long' and shortening is not what the technology produced.

wrong.A: This omits the loss of individual bargaining over hours, which the third paragraph states directly.
wrong.B: Statement II is the claim the passage separates out and rejects, since standardization is not shortening.
wrong.D: Statements I and III hold, but II attributes to the machinery the shortening the author assigns to the later statutes.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account?

choices.A: The earliest statutes were drafted by officials who had read the inspection returns
choices.B: Petitions for a shorter day grew more numerous after the statutes were passed
choices.C: In the mechanized trades a common day appeared only after the first statutes
choices.D: Some shops driven by a single shaft also employed workers paid by the piece

questions.explanation: The account depends on the chronology asserted in the first two paragraphs, that in these industries 'a standard day was already in place before the relevant statute'. Reversing that order removes the evidence the reversal of causation rests on.
