wrong.A: Officials reading the returns would fit the author's story, in which the statutes extended a standard that practice had already produced.
wrong.B: Continued petitioning after the statutes bears on the campaigns, not on when or how the standard day was first produced.
wrong.D: Mixed payment arrangements in one shop leave untouched the claim that the shaft made the hours of those attached to it indivisible.

questions.stem: The author concludes that the essay is best characterized by:

choices.A: the visible presence of a mind at work on a question
choices.B: the obligations it suspends that other forms accept
choices.C: its refusal of subjects that other forms have taken up
choices.D: the length at which a single question can be held open

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph states the conclusion: 'the essay is what is left when the obligations that constitute them are suspended', those obligations being to establish, to settle a question in advance and to be useful.

wrong.A: This is the fourth candidate, which the author calls 'nearly right' and then rejects, since what it describes 'is not a method. It is a permission.'
wrong.C: Subject matter is the first candidate to fail, and the failure is that the essay shares its subjects with the column and the sermon.
wrong.D: Length is the second candidate, refuted by counterexamples at both ends.

questions.stem: The comparison with a laboratory notebook is introduced in order to:

choices.A: show why describing the essay as thinking in public is not sufficient
choices.B: concede that the essay shares a method with empirical inquiry
choices.C: separate essays written in the first person from those that are not
choices.D: offer an example of a form whose question may change as it proceeds

questions.explanation: The notebook is brought in against the fourth candidate: it 'also exhibits a process of arriving', so exhibiting a process cannot be what distinguishes an essay.

wrong.B: The comparison is drawn to deny a shared method, since the notebook's process is answerable to a question fixed in advance.
wrong.C: The first person is the third candidate, dealt with in the preceding paragraph without reference to notebooks.
wrong.D: The notebook is the contrasting case: a notebook that wandered into another subject 'would be a bad notebook'.

questions.stem: A writer begins with a settled thesis and arranges her evidence so as to establish it. On the author's account the result is:

choices.A: a poor essay, since its refusals have been badly executed
choices.B: an essay, since subject matter does not determine the form
choices.C: not an essay, since it accepts obligations the form suspends
choices.D: an essay only if the thesis alters before the end

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph assigns such a piece to another form: 'An essay that has proved its point has become an argument; one that knew its conclusion on the first page has become an exposition.'

wrong.A: Badly executed refusals are still refusals, whereas this writer has undertaken the obligations the essay declines.
wrong.B: Subject matter is irrelevant here, and the author's test concerns the obligations a piece accepts rather than what it is about.
wrong.D: A changed question is permitted in an essay but is not a sufficient condition, and this piece has already accepted the duty to establish.

questions.stem: The author would be LEAST likely to accept which of the following as a criticism of an essay?

choices.A: It closed in a maxim where it should have closed in a difficulty
choices.B: It argued a case in a place where it should have looked at one
choices.C: It reached no conclusion that a reader could act upon
choices.D: Its conclusion was plainly in hand from the first sentence

questions.explanation: Among the suspended obligations is 'the obligation to be of use by the end', and a piece that must leave the reader better equipped 'has become advice'. The other three restate the author's own examples of the charges readers bring against an essay.

wrong.A: This is one of the three charges the final paragraph lists as proper to the form.
wrong.B: Arguing where it should have looked is named there as well, as a refusal badly executed.
wrong.D: Knowing the conclusion from the first sentence is the first charge the author says readers bring without difficulty.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's reply to the charge that the essay is parasitic?

choices.A: Readers' judgements of essays appeal only to the standards of argument and exposition
choices.B: Most essays now published are written to leave their readers better equipped
choices.C: The four candidate definitions were proposed by writers hostile to the form
choices.D: Some admired essays announce their question in the opening paragraph

questions.explanation: The reply rests on the claim that the charges readers bring 'are not borrowed standards'. If every judgement readers make turns out to be drawn from argument and exposition, the standards are borrowed after all and the charge of parasitism stands.

wrong.B: What most published essays attempt bears on current practice, not on whether the form has standards of its own.
wrong.C: The motives of those who proposed the definitions leave untouched the question of how essays are judged.
wrong.D: Announcing a question is not the same as settling it, and the author objects only to a conclusion held in advance.
